Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram in the standard oriented $3$-sphere. Use the oriented Khovanov resolution cube, crossing order, signs, and shifts fixed in the integral Khovanov construction. Over $\mathbb Q$, replace its circle algebra by $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$, with $\deg_q(1)=1$ and $\deg_q(X)=-1$, and structure maps
$$
\eta_L(1)=1,\quad \epsilon_L(1)=0,\quad \epsilon_L(X)=1,
$$
$$
m_L(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m_L(1\otimes X)=m_L(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m_L(X\otimes X)=1,
$$
$$
\Delta_L(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad \Delta_L(X)=1\otimes1+X\otimes X.
$$
For a resolution state $v$ with $k(v)$ circles, assign $A_L^{\otimes k(v)}$ and cohomological degree $i(v)=|v|-n_-$. On a tensor basis element whose circle labels are $a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)}\in\{1,X\}$, set
$$
q(v;a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)})=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{j=1}^{k(v)}\deg_q(a_j).
$$
The differential is the signed sum of the edge maps $m_L$ and $\Delta_L$. The resulting finite cochain complex is the **Lee-deformed Khovanov complex** $C_L(D;\mathbb Q)$. Its decreasing quantum filtration $F^pC_L(D;\mathbb Q)$ is spanned by basis elements of quantum degree at least $p$. Its homology with the induced filtration is the Lee homology of the diagram. The diagram-level definition does not by itself assert invariance under changing $D$.

For the empty link diagram, use its single empty resolution state and empty tensor term $\mathbb Q$ in cohomological and quantum degree $0$, with zero differential. Its induced decreasing filtration is $F^pC_L(\varnothing;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ for $p\leq0$ and $F^pC_L(\varnothing;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $p>0$.

The two equal composites in the diagram below are the Frobenius compatibility maps used on merge-split faces. The drawing names maps only; the proof checks the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$.

```tikzcd
A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"m_L"] \arrow[d,"\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & A_L \arrow[d,"\Delta_L"] \\
A_L\otimes A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m_L"'] & A_L\otimes A_L
```

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot admitting a finite regular diagram $D$ with $n$ positive crossings and no negative crossings, and let $k$ be the number of circles in its oriented resolution. Then Rasmussen’s invariant satisfies
$$
s(K)=n-k+1.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $K^\dagger$ be the reverse mirror of an oriented knot $K$. Then
$$
s(K^\dagger)=-s(K).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D_+(T_{2,3},2)$ be the positive-clasped Whitehead double of the right-handed trefoil with Hedden–Ording twist parameter $t=2$. The normalized knot Floer threshold and Rasmussen invariant satisfy
$$\tau(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=0,\qquad s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D_+(T_{2,3},2)$ be the positive-clasped Whitehead double of the right-handed trefoil in the Hedden–Ording twist convention, with companion-annulus framing two. Equivalently, start with the three-crossing positive trefoil blackboard parallel, add one negative full annulus twist, and attach the positive clasp as in the admitted sixteen-crossing code. Then
$$s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D_+(T_{2,3},2)$ be the positive-clasped Whitehead double of the right-handed trefoil with Hedden–Ording twist parameter $t=2$. The normalized knot Floer threshold and Rasmussen invariant satisfy
$$\tau(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=0,\qquad s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard oriented three-sphere,
$$
|s(K)|\le 2g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K),
$$
where $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ is the minimum genus of a connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surface in the standard four-ball with oriented boundary $K$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D_+(T_{2,3},2)$ be the positive-clasped Whitehead double of the right-handed trefoil with Hedden–Ording twist parameter $t=2$. The normalized knot Floer threshold and Rasmussen invariant satisfy
$$\tau(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=0,\qquad s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented knot $K$, let $V_K$ be its two-dimensional rational Lee homology with the diagram-independent induced decreasing quantum filtration $F^pV_K$. For a nonzero class $x\in V_K$, define its filtration level by
$$ \ell(x)=\max\{p\in\mathbb Z:x\in F^pV_K\}. $$
Set
$$ s_{\min}(K)=\min_{x\ne0}\ell(x),\qquad s_{\max}(K)=\max_{x\ne0}\ell(x), \qquad s(K)=s_{\max}(K)-1=s_{\min}(K)+1. $$
The equality of the two formulas is part of the definition’s well-definedness, supplied by the rank-two Lee filtration theorem.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with at least one component, ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and a marked point $p$ on the projected link away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

derivations.claim: **The two-saddle calculation.** Quotients commute with quotients. Two split factors anticommute because $u\wedge v=-v\wedge u$. A quotient and a split commute when the quotient carries the split difference to the corresponding output difference. These give $\kappa=1,-1,1$, respectively, for two merges, two splits and a mixed pair whose saddle types are unchanged by interchange. The remaining connected nonzero case starts with two circles and two bands between them: either order first merges and then splits. Both composites factor through the quotient identifying the two input circles. If the two band arrows point towards the same input circle, their final split differences are opposites, giving $\kappa=-1$; if they point towards different circles, the differences agree, giving $\kappa=1$. Finally, alternating endpoints on a single input circle give a split followed by a merge in either order. The quotient kills the split difference, so both composites are zero. These exhaust the cases: discard components missing both arcs, and distinguish whether each arc joins equal or distinct components; if both are self-arcs, their endpoints either alternate or do not. A spectator generator is carried identically throughout, so the computation on the incident generators proves the full exterior-map equation.

**Reversing an arrow is a gauge change.** Reverse the arrow at coordinate $i$. The unsigned edge map changes by $r(e)=-1$ on its split edges and by $r(e)=1$ on its merge edges; other edges have $r(e)=1$. The face coefficient changes by the product of these four $r$'s. For nonzero composites this follows by multiplying the two equations for the edge maps. For a zero face, the $i$-saddle is a split in one ordering and a merge in the other. Reversing its arrow reverses the left/right test defining $\kappa$, so the coefficient changes by $-1$, again the product of the $r$'s. Consequently the product of the six $\kappa$'s on a three-cube is unchanged by reversing any arrow: every edge belongs to exactly two of its faces. It suffices to check one choice of arrows for every unoriented three-saddle configuration.

**Separating a configuration.** Collapse each saddle disk to a four-valent vertex and retain the regular arcs joining its four ports. Discard vertex-free circles. This gives a planar four-valent multigraph with three vertices. If it is disconnected, one component contains just one vertex. If it has a two-edge cut, cut those edges and cap the resulting pair of ports in each piece by an arc. The original diagram is then obtained by joining the two capped marked arcs; one piece again has one vertex and the other two. The caps can be chosen in a thin neighbourhood of the cut, so they preserve the cyclic orders and inside/outside intersection test for every two-saddle face within a piece. Every resolution of the joined diagram has the circle count $k_1+k_2-1$; in the disconnected case it has count $k_1+k_2$. Thus the merge/split status of a saddle is its status in its own capped piece. A face using one saddle from each piece is an ordinary interchange with coefficient $(-1)^{b_i b_j}$ by step 1.1. The two faces using both saddles of the two-vertex piece have equal coefficients and cancel in the boundary product. If the one-vertex piece has split indicator $b_c$, the product from the four remaining faces is $(-1)^{b_c N}$, where $N$ is the sum of the split counts in the two orders of the two saddles in the other piece. Each order has the same split count, namely $(k_{\mathrm{out}}-k_{\mathrm{in}}+2)/2$. Hence $N$ is even and the boundary product is $1$. This also proves the disconnected case, using separate exterior generators rather than the marked connected sum.

**The irreducible list.** Suppose the graph is connected and has no two-edge cut. It has no loop: a loop uses two of the four ports at its vertex, and the remaining two edges would be a cut. Write $m_{ij}$ for the number of edges between vertices $i,j$. The three degree equations give $m_{12}=m_{23}=m_{31}=2$. At each vertex the two parallel edges bound a lens on one side; the remaining edges must lie on the other side, since they must reach the third vertex without crossing. Thus the planar graph has three lens faces and two triangular faces, with its cyclic orders determined up to reflection and permutation of the vertices. Resolving its three vertices gives eight choices. Permuting the vertices identifies choices having the same number of switches from the resolution into three lens circles. The four representatives, obtained by zero, one, two and three switches, have respectively these circle-and-band descriptions: three circles with three bands forming a triangle; two circles joined by two bands, with a self-band on one circle separating their attachment points; one circle with two parallel inside bands and one outside band alternating with each of them; and two circles joined by three parallel bands. This enumeration follows also by doing the switches successively: the first merges two lens circles, the second merges the remaining two circles, and the third splits their common circle. It accounts for all eight choices, without an assumption about the arrows.

**Triangle and three parallel bands.** In the triangle representative direct the three bands cyclically. A face with the third band absent is two successive merges, of coefficient $1$. With the third band performed first, the two remaining arrows point towards different circles, again giving coefficient $1$ by step 1.1. Thus all six coefficients are $1$. In the three-parallel-band representative direct all three arrows from the first circle to the second. The three bottom faces have two arrows towards the same circle and coefficient $-1$. After the third band merges the two circles, the two remaining bands are nonalternating self-bands; their two split factors anticommute, so each top face also has coefficient $-1$. In both representatives the six-face product is $1$.

**Digon with a self-band.** Place the two circles to the left and right, draw the two joining bands above and below, and draw the self-band across the left circle, separating the upper and lower attachment points. Direct both joining bands towards the right circle. The face of the two joining bands before the self-band is a same-head interchange and has coefficient $-1$. After the self-band, those bands form a tree on three circles and the corresponding face has coefficient $1$. The two faces involving the self-band before the other joining band are ordinary mixed interchanges and have coefficient $1$. After a joining band is performed, the other joining band and the self-band have alternating endpoints. The two resulting zero faces are reflections across the horizontal midline, with the self-band arrow retained and the two equally directed joining arrows exchanged. Reflection reverses the inside/outside oriented-intersection test, so their $\kappa$'s are opposite. Their product is $-1$, cancelling the single nonzero coefficient $-1$. The total product is $1$, for either direction of the self-band arrow.

**Two inside bands and an outside band.** List the endpoints clockwise as $c,a,b,c,b,a$, where $a,b$ are the two parallel inside bands and $c$ is outside. Direct $a,b$ upwards. Their bottom face consists of two splits and has coefficient $-1$. After performing $c$, their heads lie on the same one of the two resulting circles; their top face is a same-head interchange and has coefficient $-1$. The faces $(a,c)$ before $b$ and $(b,c)$ before $a$ are zero faces with the same inside-arrow direction and the same outside arrow, hence have equal coefficients. Their product is $1$. In the two remaining faces, performing the other inside band has separated the endpoints of $c$; the two events are an ordinary merge and split with coefficient $1$. Thus the six-face product is again $1$, for either direction of $c$. Steps 3.1–4.3 and arrow reversal in step 2.1 prove that every three-cube has boundary product $\prod\kappa=1$. Consequently $\phi=-\kappa$ also has boundary product $1$, because there are six faces.

**Constructing the signs.** Induct on cube dimension $n$. For $n=0$ there are no signs; for $n=1$ choose the only edge sign $1$. For the induction step construct signs on the lower face $v_n=0$, set every edge in direction $n$ to $1$, and define an upper-face edge in direction $i<n$ by $\epsilon_i(v,1)=\phi_{i,n}(v)\epsilon_i(v,0)$. This enforces each vertical face product. For an upper face in directions $i,j<n$, multiply the six face equations for its three-cube with direction $n$: the lower face and four vertical faces already have their prescribed products, while the six prescribed products multiply to $1$ by step 4.3. Therefore the upper face has its prescribed product too. The resulting differential has square zero: on a nonzero face the two unsigned composites differ by $\kappa$, while their signed coefficient ratio is $-\kappa$; on a zero face both composites vanish. Every operation in this induction is a finite multiplication of signs.

**Comparison.** If $\epsilon,\epsilon'$ realize the same face products, their quotient $\rho(e)=\epsilon'(e)/\epsilon(e)$ has product $1$ around every face. Give the lowest vertex sign $1$, and give any other vertex the product of $\rho$ along a monotone path to it. Two such paths differ by interchanging adjacent coordinate changes; each interchange is a square and leaves the product unchanged. Therefore these vertex signs are well-defined and their ratio across an edge is $\rho(e)$. Multiplying every state module by its vertex sign gives a chain isomorphism. These scalar maps preserve both normalized gradings and, when a mark is supplied, commute with its marked action by [F2]. This proves all the assertions.

citations.quote: Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with at least one component, ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and a marked point $p$ on the projected link away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

Let a finite planar resolution cube be equipped with an arrow at each crossing, transported to its saddle edges while resolving the other disjoint crossing disks, and use the odd exterior merge and split maps. There is a function assigning a sign to every edge such that the resulting signed differential squares to zero over the integers. More precisely, one can prescribe the face products on all faces, including faces whose two composites vanish, as follows. On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. On a zero-composite face the two saddle arcs have alternating endpoints on one circle, one arc inside and one outside; put them in the standard two-chord picture by an orientation-preserving planar isotopy and rotate so that the inside arrow points upwards and set $\kappa=1$ when the outside arrow points left, and $\kappa=-1$ when it points right. Then the prescribed product of the four edge signs is $-\kappa$. These prescriptions are consistent, and two edge assignments realizing the same prescriptions are related by a vertexwise sign change. All the constructions are finite and choice-free. The vertexwise comparison commutes with the marked right $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action.

derivations.claim: **A cancellation identity over any ring.** Suppose a cochain differential $d$ on $M=A\oplus B\oplus R$ has a degree-one block $b:A\to B$ which is an isomorphism. Set $h|_B=b^{-1}$ and $h|_{A\oplus R}=0$. Then $h^2=0$ and $hdh=h$. Consequently $E=1-dh-hd$ is a projection commuting with $d$: expansion using $d^2=h^2=0$ and $hdh=h$ gives $E^2=E$ and $dE=Ed$. Writing $j:R\to M$ and $q:M\to R$ for the direct-sum maps, set $i=Ej=j-hdj$, $p=qE=q-qdh$, and $d_R=q(d-dhd)j$. The $A$-coordinate of a vector in $\operatorname{im}E$ is minus $hd$ of its $R$-coordinate, and its $B$-coordinate is zero; hence $q:\operatorname{im}E\to R$ and $Ej$ are inverse. Thus $pi=1$, $ip=E$, $di=id_R$, $pd=d_Rp$, and $1-ip=dh+hd$. These identities also give $d_R^2=0$. If the blocks and their inverse are right-module maps, so are all these maps. This calculation applies to entire finite exterior cubes at once; their differentials are included in $d$, rather than omitted as spectators.

**The RII four-state model.** Call the straight matching $I$ and the cup-cap matching $U$. Rotate the disk and order the crossing whose smoothing pair is $(I,U)$ first, followed by the crossing whose smoothing pair is $(U,I)$. This order refers to the geometric smoothings; for either orientation of the two strands the pair contains one oriented positive and one oriented negative crossing. The local states $00,01,10,11$ are $U,I,U\sqcup z,U$. In state $10$ label the circle through the upper arc $a$, the small circle $z$, and the circle through the lower arc $c$; the exterior closure may identify $a$ and $c$. These labels therefore denote actual generators, with that equality imposed when applicable. At $00\to10$ the map is the split $(a-z)\wedge(-)$ after choosing its lift; at $10\to11$ the quotient identifies $z$ with $c$. Each edge has its prescribed sign, which is $\pm1$ and may depend on $v$. In $10$ set $Y=z-c$ and write $L=\Lambda W$, $K=Y\wedge\Lambda W$, where $W$ is the circle group of $U$. The quotient $10\to11$ is the identity on $L$ and zero on $K$. The $K$-coefficient of $00\to10$ is minus the identity, because $a-z=(a-c)-Y$. This remains true when $a=c$. Thus both indicated blocks are invertible right-module blocks for every exterior closure.

**The merge curl.** Write $W_v$ for the old circle group and $c_v$ for the circle through the curl's continuing arc. The two local states are $\Lambda(W_v\oplus\mathbb Zz)$ and $\Lambda W_v$, with merge quotient $m(z)=m(c_v)=c_v$. Put $Y=z-c_v$ and decompose the first state as $L_v\oplus K_v$, where $L_v=\Lambda W_v$ and $K_v=Y\wedge\Lambda W_v$. The merge is the identity $L_v\to\Lambda W_v$ and kills $K_v$. External edges preserve both summands. Indeed a merge takes $Y$ to its new $Y$, while a split takes $Y$ to the new $Y$ up to a multiple of its own split difference; that extra term vanishes when wedged with the same difference. On $L$ the external maps are the old maps. On $K$, identifying $Y\wedge w$ with $w$ negates each external split and leaves each merge unchanged. Put $\sigma(v)=(k(v)-k(0)+|v|)/2$. It is an integer, unchanged by a merge and increased by one by a split. Thus $w\mapsto(-1)^{\sigma(v)}Y\wedge w$ identifies $K$ with the old complex. The other two summands cancel by step 1.1, using the signed merge pivot and its inverse. With the ordinary cube ordering its pivot coefficient can be taken $(-1)^{|v|}$. The normalization makes the survivor's cohomological and quantum degrees those of the old diagram: the extra small circle and extra exterior generator change the local quantum degree by $-1$, cancelling the positive-curl shift $+1$.

**The two RII cancellations.** First cancel $L_{10}\to U_{11}$ by step 1.1. Its inverse is the signed inclusion using no $z$. The correction $-dhd$ does not alter the $00\to K_{10}$ block, since external edges preserve $L$ and the local outgoing arrow from $L$ lands only in $11$. That block is still the signed minus identity, so cancel $U_{00}\to K_{10}$. The survivor is $I_{01}$. Its exterior differential is unchanged: after the first cancellation no differential from $I_{01}$ enters $K$, since its only local outgoing edge was to the cancelled $11$ and the correction factors through $L$, which has no $K$-component. Consequently the second cancellation contributes no correction on $I_{01}$. The local height is one, the pair adds one negative and one positive crossing, and hence the homological shift is $1-1=0$ and the quantum shift is $1+(1-2)=0$. This proves the normalized equivalence.

**The split curl.** Here the local arrow is $\Lambda W_v\to\Lambda(W_v\oplus\mathbb Zz)$, $w\mapsto Y\wedge w$, with either overall sign allowed. Use the same decomposition $L\oplus K$. The split is an isomorphism onto $K$; $L$ survives. Choose the crossing-edge coefficient $(-1)^{|v|+\sigma(v)}$ when the external edges have their old coefficients. Across an external merge this coefficient changes sign, and across a split it is unchanged. Since the unsigned curl split commutes with the former and anticommutes with the latter, every mixed square anticommutes. Cancel its isomorphism onto $K$ by step 1.1. The surviving $L$ has its old differential and right action. It is at local height one; the negative crossing increases $n_-$ by one, so its normalized cohomological degree is unchanged. Its additional circle contributes quantum degree $+1$, its local height contributes $+1$, and the negative crossing contributes $-2$, again giving shift zero. The formulas include both directions of the move, since the inclusion and projection are homotopy inverses.

**Module maps, signs and reduction.** The mark is outside the disk, so it is never the small circle $z$. In the displayed decompositions a right multiplication appends an old generator. Coefficient projections in $z$ and $Y=z-c$, the inclusions, and multiplication by a left split difference therefore commute with that right action. All pivots, their signed inverses and the maps in step 1.1 are module-linear. Different admissible edge signs are accommodated by [F2]. Reversing a saddle arrow negates its split map and is absorbed in that edge coefficient; changing strand orientations changes only the normalized crossing shifts, already checked for R1 and RII. Rotations simply relabel the generators and disk ports. Modulo two all displayed signs become one, exterior products become commuting square-zero circle labels, and $z-c$ becomes $z+c$. Merge, split, inclusion, coefficient projection and the formula $d-dhd$ reduce to precisely the even cancellation operations. Thus the maps, inverses and homotopies have the asserted comparison, for every closure and orientation.

citations.quote: Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with at least one component, ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and a marked point $p$ on the projected link away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

Let a finite planar resolution cube be equipped with an arrow at each crossing, transported to its saddle edges while resolving the other disjoint crossing disks, and use the odd exterior merge and split maps. There is a function assigning a sign to every edge such that the resulting signed differential squares to zero over the integers. More precisely, one can prescribe the face products on all faces, including faces whose two composites vanish, as follows. On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. On a zero-composite face the two saddle arcs have alternating endpoints on one circle, one arc inside and one outside; put them in the standard two-chord picture by an orientation-preserving planar isotopy and rotate so that the inside arrow points upwards and set $\kappa=1$ when the outside arrow points left, and $\kappa=-1$ when it points right. Then the prescribed product of the four edge signs is $-\kappa$. These prescriptions are consistent, and two edge assignments realizing the same prescriptions are related by a vertexwise sign change. All the constructions are finite and choice-free. The vertexwise comparison commutes with the marked right $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action.

For a finite planar odd resolution cube with the prescribed full face signs, a Reidemeister I or II move supported away from the marked point induces a normalized bigraded chain homotopy equivalence over the right ring $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$. The equivalence, inverse and contraction are finite integer matrices in exterior quotients, exterior products, and projections to the two coefficients of a small-circle generator. Their reductions modulo two are the corresponding even Khovanov cancellation maps. The result holds for every exterior closure of the move disk and every orientation of its strands, and is choice-free.

For finite based diagrams differing by Reidemeister III in a disk missing the mark, their normalized odd complexes, with the prescribed full face signs, are bigraded chain homotopy equivalent over the right ring $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$. The equivalences and homotopies are integral and reduce modulo two to the even local cancellation equivalence. They apply to every exterior closure, including closures in which several local arcs belong to the same resolution circle. Together with the marked Reidemeister I and II contractions this proves invariance under every finite based Reidemeister sequence. No choice axiom is needed for these finite constructions.

derivations.claim: **An odd saddle as one more cube direction.** Replace its two local smoothings by an auxiliary crossing, ordered after the actual crossings. By [F2] its full cube has edge signs. The auxiliary edges form maps $g_v$ between its lower and upper faces; the mixed square equations say $d_1g+gd_0=0$, where $g$ preserves the actual resolution height. Put $F_v=(-1)^{|v|}g_v$. Since an actual edge increases $|v|$ by one, this identity becomes $d_1F=Fd_0$. The side-face restrictions are admissible assignments for the actual endpoint diagrams; use [F2]'s vertex-sign maps to identify them with any chosen admissible endpoint assignments. Every $g_v$ is an odd saddle, so commutes with the right marked action. The factor $(-1)^{|v|}$ and the vertex signs do too. Modulo two the construction is exactly the ordinary even saddle map. The auxiliary crossing is used only to choose coefficients, not included in the endpoint normalization. For a merge the circle count decreases by one at unchanged exterior degree; for a split it increases by one and exterior degree increases by one. Thus both maps have quantum degree $-1$ and cohomological degree zero.

**Odd birth and death signs.** A birth appends a generator $z$ for a small disjoint circle and uses the inclusion $\Lambda W\to\Lambda(W\oplus\mathbb Zz)$, without inserting $z$. External maps preserve this subalgebra, so the inclusion is a chain map with unchanged edge assignment. For a death use $(-1)^{\sigma(v)}\iota_z$, where $\iota_z$ is exterior contraction with the coefficient functional of $z$. It commutes with external merge quotients. For a split with difference $u$ not involving $z$, $\iota_z(u\wedge w)=-u\wedge\iota_z(w)$; the increase of $\sigma$ cancels that minus sign. Thus this is also a chain map. The mark is not $z$, and $\iota_z(w\wedge Z_p)=\iota_z(w)\wedge Z_p$, so both maps are marked right-module maps. A birth adds one circle and no exterior generator, giving quantum degree $+1$. A nonzero death removes a circle and one exterior generator, giving degree $-1+2=+1$. Modulo two these are the unit and counit of the even algebra.

**The deformed circle coordinates.** Work over $\mathbb Z[h]$, retaining the marked $\mathbb R$-action. Write a small circle first as $1\otimes w_1+X\otimes w_X$. If $x$ is the dot on the arc from which it splits, the split has coordinates $u\mapsto((x-h)u,u)$, since $\Delta(u)=1\otimes(X-h)u+X\otimes u$. A merge into an arc with dot $y$ is $(w_1,w_X)\mapsto w_1+yw_X$. Opposite saddles satisfy $ts=x+y-h$. For distinct circles the equation is $\Delta m(a\otimes b)=Xa\otimes b+a\otimes Xb-h a\otimes b$: substituting $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$ gives respectively $1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h1\otimes1$, $X\otimes X$, $X\otimes X$, $hX\otimes X$ on both sides. For a single circle it is $m\Delta(u)=(2X-h)u$. Dot operators commute with saddles by $m(Xa,b)=Xm(a,b)$ and $\Delta(Xa)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(a)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(a)$, verified on $1,X$.

**Deformed RI and RII.** A merge curl is $(u,v)\mapsto u+Xv$. Its survivor inclusion is $w\mapsto(-Xw,w)$, its projection is $(u,v)\mapsto v$, and its contraction on the target is $w\mapsto(w,0)$. A split curl is $w\mapsto((X-h)w,w)$; its survivor inclusion is $u\mapsto(u,0)$, its projection is $(u,v)\mapsto u-(X-h)v$, and its contraction is $(u,v)\mapsto v$. Substitution gives $pi=1$ and $1-ip=dh+hd$ in both cases. For RII use states $U,I,U\sqcup\mu,U$ at $00,01,10,11$ and the signed differential $d^0(u)=(su,(x-h)u,u)$, $d^1(v,w_1,w_X)=tv-w_1-yw_X$. Put $i(v)=(v,tv,0)$, $p(v,w_1,w_X)=v-sw_X$, $h^1(v,w_1,w_X)=w_X$, $h^2(z)=(0,-z,0)$. The equation $ts=x+y-h$ gives $d^2=0$, $di=pd=0$, $pi=1$. In local degree one, $dh+hd$ is $(v,w_1,w_X)\mapsto(sw_X,w_1-tv+(x+y-h)w_X,w_X)$, exactly $1-ip$; in local degrees zero and two it is the identity. These are actual inverse maps and homotopies. The RI and RII normalization checks are the same circle-height calculations in [F3], since $h$ has quantum degree $-2$.

**An $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$-linear localized contraction.** Put $S=\mathbb Z[h,h^{-1}]$ and $A=X$, $B=h-X$. Direct substitution gives $A^2=hA$, $B^2=hB$, $AB=0$, $\Delta(A)=A\otimes A$, $\Delta(B)=-B\otimes B$. These are an $S$-basis of the localized circle algebra. Every enhanced state fixes a label on every original diagram segment. An edge is nonzero precisely when all its incident labels agree; its coefficient is then $h$ or $\pm1$, an $S$-unit. At an all-equal crossing both smoothings are compatible; at any other crossing admitting a compatible smoothing only that smoothing is allowed. Thus each connected enhanced-state summand is a Boolean cube on its free coordinates. Divide its edge coefficients by the standard cube signs. The square-zero equation says that the products along the two sides of every square agree. Rescale vertices by their path products, which are path-independent by swapping adjacent coordinates. This identifies the summand with a tensor product of copies of $S\xrightarrow{1}S$. A nonempty product contracts by the inverse on its first identity factor, with the tensor differential signs. Throughout a summand the marked label is fixed, so $X$ acts uniformly by $h$ or $0$; the rescaling and contraction commute with that action. This is therefore a contraction over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$, not just over $S$.

**Deformed RIII with both pivots.** Use ports and matchings $I,E_1,E_2,P=E_1E_2,Q=E_2E_1$ as in [F3], and order the three local crossings in the word $121$. The states are $I$; $(E_1^a,E_2^b,E_1^c)$; $(P,E_1\sqcup\mu,Q)$; $E_1$. Let $u:E_1\to P$ insert $E_2$ below, $v:E_2\to P$ insert $E_1$ above, $w:E_1\to Q$ insert $E_2$ above, and $z:E_2\to Q$ insert $E_1$ below. With the small-circle coordinates first, $d^1(a,b,c)=(-ua+vb,-(x-h)a+(y-h)c,-a+c,wc-zb)$. Here $x,y$ are the dots on the bottom and top arcs from which $\mu$ splits. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with at least one component, ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and a marked point $p$ on the projected link away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.

On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. derivations.claim: **A right-linear reduced decomposition.** At each state let $V$ be the circle group, $Z$ its marked generator, and $U=\ker(\operatorname{aug}:V\to\mathbb Z)$, where every circle has augmentation one. The vectors $Y_j=Z_j-Z$ for unmarked circles are a basis of $U$, and $V=U\oplus\mathbb ZZ$. Thus $\Lambda V=\Lambda U\otimes\mathbb A$ as a right module, by $u\otimes1\mapsto u$, $u\otimes X\mapsto u\wedge Z$. A merge preserves augmentation and takes the marked generator to the marked generator. For a split choose the lift of its old marked generator to the new marked generator; if the marked circle is unaffected this is the usual lift. This lift also preserves augmentation, and the split difference belongs to $U$ in the target. Hence in these coordinates every edge acts as its reduced exterior quotient or split on $\Lambda U$, tensored with the identity of $\mathbb A$. This is an equality of maps on both $u$ and $u\wedge Z$, not merely an unmarked abelian-group splitting.

citations.quote: Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with at least one component, ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and a marked point $p$ on the projected link away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

Let a finite planar resolution cube be equipped with an arrow at each crossing, transported to its saddle edges while resolving the other disjoint crossing disks, and use the odd exterior merge and split maps. There is a function assigning a sign to every edge such that the resulting signed differential squares to zero over the integers. More precisely, one can prescribe the face products on all faces, including faces whose two composites vanish, as follows. On a face with nonzero composites let $\kappa\in\{1,-1\}$ be their relative commutation sign. On a zero-composite face the two saddle arcs have alternating endpoints on one circle, one arc inside and one outside; put them in the standard two-chord picture by an orientation-preserving planar isotopy and rotate so that the inside arrow points upwards and set $\kappa=1$ when the outside arrow points left, and $\kappa=-1$ when it points right. Then the prescribed product of the four edge signs is $-\kappa$. These prescriptions are consistent, and two edge assignments realizing the same prescriptions are related by a vertexwise sign change. All the constructions are finite and choice-free. The vertexwise comparison commutes with the marked right $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$-action.

derivations.claim: **The zero-face cyclic-order test, with both outside placements.** Name the inside arc $a$ and the outside arc $b$, and write their directed endpoints as $a_-,a_+,b_-,b_+$. Give their common circle the positive boundary orientation of its bounded disk. The endpoints alternate, so the two possible cyclic words starting at $a_-$ are $W_+=(a_-,b_-,a_+,b_+)$ and $W_-=(a_-,b_+,a_+,b_-)$. Put $\chi(W_+)=1$ and $\chi(W_-)=-1$. The precise calibration must include both possible placements of the unbounded face on the outside-arc side: they need not be related by a planar isotopy fixing all endpoint labels. Straighten the circle locally at its four endpoints, with inside $a$ directed from South to North, and put the endpoints of $b$ at West and East. Read the outside arrow at an endpoint germ, as in the stipulated standard picture, rather than at a midpoint of its exterior route. There are four cases. If $b$ runs from West to East above the circle, it enters its head at East leftwards, the cyclic word is $W_-$, and $\kappa=1$. If it runs from West to East below the circle, the head germ is still leftwards, its word is still $W_-$, and $\kappa=1$. If $b$ runs from East to West above the circle, it enters West rightwards, its word is $W_+$, and $\kappa=-1$. If it runs from East to West below the circle, its head germ remains rightwards, its word remains $W_+$, and $\kappa=-1$. The same direction is obtained at the tail germ: outgoing at West is leftwards and outgoing at East rightwards. Thus all four placements give the single formula $\kappa=-\chi$. This table also treats the two possible faces on each side of the circle cut by its surgery arc. Straightening an endpoint germ uses only its transverse attachment on the indicated side and does not change which directed endpoint it is; no isotopy exchanging the two outside-face placements is assumed.

**Changing the omitted point.** Consider the same zero-face circle on the oriented sphere. Its two complementary sides contain its two surgery arcs. If the two omitted points are on the same side, both planar boundary orientations agree and both presentations call the same arc inside. Their cyclic word and $\kappa$ agree by step 1.1. If the omitted points are on opposite sides, the inside/outside names are exchanged and the positive bounded-side boundary orientation is reversed: the boundary orientations of the two sides of an oriented surface are opposite. Both changes are necessary. For example, an old word $W_+=(a_-,b_-,a_+,b_+)$, read in the reverse orientation starting at $b_-$, is $(b_-,a_-,b_+,a_+)$, which is the new word $W_+$ when $b$ is the new inside arc and $a$ the new outside arc. An old word $W_-=(a_-,b_+,a_+,b_-)$ becomes $(b_-,a_+,b_+,a_-)$, which is the new word $W_-$. Hence $\chi$, and therefore $\kappa$, is unchanged in this case too. This is the full two-case calculation; exchanging only the names without reversing the boundary orientation would give an incorrect sign. The same argument applies to an arbitrary orientation-preserving spherical change of coordinates by transporting the circle and its two sides first.

**Naturality of every unsigned saddle.** At state $v$ let $P_v$ send each circle generator to that same spherical circle in the other chart. It is a bijection of bases. For a merge quotient $q$, both $P_{v+e}q$ and $q'P_v$ send the two merging generators to the same merged generator and fix every spectator. Thus their exterior extensions agree. For a split, transport the arrow and its ordered output circles. Then $P_{v+e}$ carries the difference $C_1-C_2$ to $C'_1-C'_2$. Choose the transported lift $j'$ of the split input. On every wedge $z$ one has $\Lambda P_{v+e}((C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda j(z))=(C'_1-C'_2)\wedge\Lambda j'(\Lambda P_v(z))$. The alternative lift gives the same expression by [F1]. Circle order changes are absorbed by the exterior relabelling, including their actual wedge signs. Thus the two unsigned composites on every face are conjugate by invertible relabellings. On a nonzero face their relative commutation sign $\kappa$ is consequently unchanged. On a zero face it is unchanged by step 2.1. All face products prescribed by [F2] therefore agree in the two charts.

**Odd chain isomorphisms and their actual inverse.** Choose a full admissible assignment in the first chart using [F2] and give each corresponding edge of the second chart the same sign. By step 3.1 these are full admissible signs in the second chart, and $P_o=\bigoplus_v\Lambda P_v$ intertwines their signed differentials. Its inverse is $\bigoplus_v\Lambda(P_v^{-1})$, so both composites are exactly the identity; the chain homotopies for an inverse are zero. If the second chart instead has independently chosen full admissible signs, divide those signs by the transported signs. The quotient has product one on every face, including the zero faces. Fix the lowest vertex sign to be one and assign each other vertex the product of the edge quotients along a monotone path. The square equations make this independent of the path, since adjacent coordinate exchanges connect all monotone paths. Multiplication by the resulting scalar at each vertex conjugates the transported differential to the chosen one. Compose this diagonal map with $P_o$. Its inverse is the inverse relabelling followed by the same scalar signs in the inverse order. This proves the asserted isomorphism for the independently chosen assignments, without claiming independence for arbitrary weak square-compatible assignments.

**Marked linearity and gradings.** Relabelling carries the marked generator $Z_p$ to the marked generator $Z'_p$. Hence $P_o(z\wedge Z_p)=P_o(z)\wedge Z'_p$. Vertexwise scalar signs commute with this right action too. Both the odd map and its inverse are thus $\mathbb A$-linear. An orientation-preserving surface chart preserves the signed crossing, its designated 0/1 smoothing and its over/under information. It consequently preserves $n_+,n_-,|v|,k(v)$; relabelling preserves exterior degree. The formula in [F1] then proves preservation of both normalized gradings. Vertexwise signs have degree zero. There is no semilinear substitution $X\mapsto-X$ in these maps.

**The integral Bar–Natan map.** On each state relabel the tensor factors by their spherical circles and keep the labels $1,X$ and the coefficient $h$ unchanged. Commutativity of multiplication and cocommutativity of comultiplication make this independent of a tensor-factor ordering. For a merge, split, birth or death the relabelling intertwines the operations because their input and output circles and all coefficients in the formulas of [F1] agree. In particular it intertwines every cube edge. The crossing order has been kept, so the ordinary cube edge signs agree as well. This yields a chain isomorphism $P_h$ with inverse the inverse tensor-factor relabelling. It takes multiplication by the marked $X$ to multiplication by the target marked $X$, and fixes $h$, so is $\mathbb R$-linear. The grading check is the same state-shift calculation as in step 5.1, with unchanged circle labels. Both inverse composites are identities with zero homotopies.

**The common reduction and the local maps.** Modulo two all vertex signs and exterior reorder signs are one. The reduced odd map sends a selected subset of circles to exactly the same spherical subset in the other chart. After setting $(2,h)=0$, the Bar–Natan map sends the tensor state with those $X$-labels to that same subset. Under the comparison of [F1] these maps are identical on every basis state, including its marked action. Thus $P_h f=f'P_o$ holds exactly after the specified quotients, not merely up to homotopy. The inverse maps satisfy the same calculation. Since $P_h$ is already an integral marked-module chain isomorphism, localizing at $h$ retains its explicit inverse and zero homotopies. This verifies all local-map conditions, with the full asserted degrees and module structures, whenever the endpoint triples satisfy the LEO-object hypotheses; it does not assert rank-one localization for arbitrary multi-component links. The only sign assignment and comparison constructions used finite cube paths and finite multiplications, so require no choice axiom.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D,D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams
([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]), regarded as decorated immersed oriented
$4$-valent planar graphs. Then $D$ and $D'$ are **planar isotopic** when there
is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy
$\Phi\colon\mathbb R^2\times I\to\mathbb R^2$, with $\Phi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and
each $\Phi_t$ an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]), such that
$\Phi_1$ carries the decorated graph of $D$ to that of $D'$: it maps the image
curve of $D$ bijectively onto that of $D'$, carries the over/under datum of
every double point to the over/under datum of the corresponding double point,
and preserves the strand orientations. A **planar isotopy of diagrams** is a
family $D_t=\Phi_t(D_0)$ for such a jointly smooth ambient isotopy $\Phi$,
with the decorations transported by $\Phi_t$. The source curves are immersed,
not embedded in the plane at their crossings.

Planar isotopies are admitted as moves in the Reidemeister theorem: they carry
a regular projection between the exceptional times of a general-position
isotopy of the link, and no crossing of the diagram is created or destroyed
along them. They are listed separately from the three local moves
([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]), of which R1 and R2 create or destroy crossings, while R3 rearranges three
existing crossings and preserves their number.
Composing planar isotopies and composing them with the local moves gives the
equivalence relation generated by the moves, and every single move below is
understood up to planar isotopy outside its small disk.

derivations.claim: **Straighten only a crossing-free marked germ.** Translate the mark to $z=0$ and rotate its oriented tangent to the positive real axis, by paths of positive planar similarities. Since the mark is a regular non-double point, there is a small disk meeting the diagram in just one arc. The inverse-function theorem expresses that arc as $y=f(x)$, where $f(0)=f'(0)=0$. It can be straightened by the supported shear $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y-t\chi(x,y)f(x))$, $0\le t\le1$: choose a cutoff equal to one near the smaller graph segment and supported in a rectangle of width and height comparable to a sufficiently small $r$. There $f(x)=O(r^2)$, whereas $\partial_y\chi=O(r^{-1})$. Thus $1-t(\partial_y\chi)f>0$ after shrinking $r$. Each vertical coordinate map is strictly increasing and the identity outside a compact interval, so each shear is a global orientation-preserving diffeomorphism; its inverse is smooth by its positive vertical derivative. Choose nested neighborhoods so that after this shear the diagram in $|z|<2r$ is the real diameter and no other strand meets that disk. Shrink $r<1$ if necessary. The part not in the real interval $|x|<r$ consequently satisfies $|z|\ge r$. All these isotopies merely transport the mark and crossing decorations; their local supports meet no crossing.

**An actual rotation recharting.** Choose $0<\epsilon<\min(r/4,1/4)$ and set $a=i\epsilon$. On the oriented stereographic sphere use the fractional linear coordinate $$w=-\frac{1+\overline a z}{z-a}.$$ The matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-\overline a&-1\\1&-a\end{smallmatrix}\right)/\sqrt{1+|a|^2}$ is unitary with determinant one: its columns have norm one and scalar product zero, and its unnormalized determinant is $1+|a|^2$. Hence its fractional linear action is the action of an orientation-preserving rotation of the round two-sphere. Its omitted old point is $a$, which lies off the real germ in the marked disk, hence in a face adjacent to the mark and outside all crossing disks. The old omitted point $\infty$ is sent to $-\overline a$, which is an ordinary point of the new chart. The map is smooth on the entire spherical diagram and preserves the oriented local crossing charts and all transported decorations.

**A quantitative exterior closing arc.** For every old diagram point outside the interval $|x|<r$, step 1.1 and the triangle inequality give $$|w|\le\frac{1+\epsilon|z|}{|z|-\epsilon}\le B:=\frac{1+\epsilon r}{r-\epsilon}.$$ The second inequality holds because the rational function has derivative $-(1+\epsilon^2)/(s-\epsilon)^2<0$ for $s\ge r$. The inequality $B<1/\epsilon$ is equivalent to $2\epsilon<r(1-\epsilon^2)$, which follows from $\epsilon<r/4$ and $\epsilon<1/4$. Choose a real $R$ strictly between $B$ and $1/\epsilon$. On the real germ $$|w(x)|^2=\frac{1+\epsilon^2x^2}{x^2+\epsilon^2},$$ whose derivative with respect to $x^2$ is $(\epsilon^4-1)/(x^2+\epsilon^2)^2<0$. Since the value at $x=0$ is $1/\epsilon^2>R^2$ and at $|x|=r$ is at most $B^2<R^2$, the circle $|w|=R$ meets that germ at exactly $x=\pm c$, with $$c^2=\frac{1-R^2\epsilon^2}{R^2-\epsilon^2},\qquad 0<c<r.$$ Both intersections are transverse, since $c\ne0$ and the derivative just computed is nonzero there. The only diagram points outside the closed disk $|w|\le R$ form the single open arc parametrized by $-c<x<c$; its closure contains the mark and has no crossing. The image is a round circular arc, because a fractional linear map sends a circle on the sphere to a circle and its pole $i\epsilon$ is not on the real circle. Every other strand and every crossing is strictly inside the disk. Thus this is the claimed exterior closing arc, with uniform crossing-free neighborhoods of it and of its two cut points.

**Record spatial coordinate identifications.** A planar shear in step 1.1 lifts on a spatial projection chart by $(x,y,h)\mapsto(\Phi_t(x,y),h)$. Its compact planar support can also be cut off in height on a larger box containing the link: use its compactly supported time-dependent planar velocity multiplied by a height cutoff equal to one on that box, with zero height velocity. The flow is complete, agrees with the displayed lift near the link, and extends by the identity to $S^3$. The initial translations and rotations have their usual orientation-preserving similarity lifts and smooth conformal extensions at the point at infinity. For the rechart, realize the projection sphere as the equator of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R$. If $Q\in SO(3)$ is the rotation from step 2.1, then $(v,s)\mapsto(Qv,s)$ is an orthogonal determinant-one map of $\mathbb R^4$ preserving $S^3$ and preserving its orientation. On the equatorial collar it transports the projection direction, the signed height, and the over/under datum. The Euclidean projection and the equatorial product projection require an explicit chart identification. Write $q=(0,0,1,0)$ for the spatial stereographic point, $z=x+iy$, $$X(z)=\frac{(2x,2y,|z|^2-1)}{1+|z|^2},\qquad d(z)=\frac{2}{1+|z|^2}.$$ Standard inverse spatial stereographic projection is $$E(z,h)=\frac{(2x,2y,|z|^2+h^2-1,2h)}{1+|z|^2+h^2}.$$ The product-collar chart with the same first normal derivative is $$T(z,h)=\bigl(\sqrt{1-d(z)^2h^2}\,X(z),d(z)h\bigr).$$ On $h=0$ these charts agree and have identical full first derivatives: both normal derivatives are $d(z)e_4$, while their tangential derivatives are those of $X$. On a compact planar neighborhood containing the diagram, the coordinate transition $\Psi=E^{-1}T$ therefore satisfies $\Psi-\mathrm{id}=O(h^2)$ and $D\Psi-I=O(|h|)$ uniformly. Choose a slightly larger compact planar box and cut off this difference there and in a height slab $|h|<\eta$. A height cutoff has derivative $O(\eta^{-1})$, multiplying an error $O(\eta^2)$; thus the resulting global compactly supported displacement $V$ has $\|DV\|<1/2$ for small $\eta$. Every $\mathrm{id}+tV$ is injective by the Lipschitz bound, is a local orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, and is onto: it is proper, its image is closed and open, and the plane-height space is connected. Its inverse is smooth by the inverse-function theorem. This is an actual ambient coordinate isotopy, extending by the identity to $S^3$. First shrink any existing Euclidean height realization by a positive constant so it lies where both cutoffs equal one. Height scaling is an embedding isotopy: at every double point both branch heights are multiplied by the same positive factor. The new spatial representative is then exactly $T(z,h)$, with product-collar base coordinate $z$ and signed height $d(z)h$. Because $d(z)>0$, at a double point it preserves the strict over/under ordering. Hence the displayed Euclidean diagram is identified with the product-collar diagram by this explicit spatial map; they are not assumed literally equal off the equator. These are actual marked link isotopies and coordinate identifications with specified endpoints. Composing these coordinate maps and height isotopies gives the asserted spatial identification; no claim that the rotation is a planar isotopy is used.

**Compatibility with protected long ends.** The exterior arc and two slightly longer joining collars have injective projection and are disjoint in projection from the remaining compact part, except at their adjacent ends. On a narrow planar neighborhood of that arc its spatial height is a smooth function $h(x,y)$, extended from the arc in tubular coordinates. A supported vertical translation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,z-t\eta(x,y)h(x,y))$ sets its height to zero on a smaller neighborhood; this is a diffeomorphism for every $t$, since its derivative in $z$ is one. It cannot reverse an over/under ordering, and there are no double points in its smaller marked support. Choose the joining neighborhoods slightly longer before cutting, so the resulting cut collars are fixed smooth product collars. The remaining diagram is a compact tangle in the round disk, and the single planar exterior arc is its marked closure. These are precisely endpoint data that may be retained as protected long endpoints in a relative movie construction. Every operation has preserved the transported mark, and none passes it through a crossing. Finite composition proves the assertion, including its recorded spatial coordinate identification. No algebraic comparison of the two charts, no arbitrary mark-slide identity, and no purely planar comparison have been assumed.
